common_name: Ogon Nishiki Asiatic Jasmine (Variegated Gold-and-Green Groundcover Vine)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring or fall in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Ogon Nishiki is slower and more compact than straight-species asiatic jasmine, so space plants closer and expect a longer fill-in period.

directions: Ogon Nishiki is a variegated sport of asiatic jasmine, grown for small, oval leaves irregularly splashed and mottled in cream, gold, and green rather than the solid dark green of the straight species. Cooler weather intensifies the variegation, often flushing the cream portions of the leaf with pink to rosy-red tones through fall and winter, an effect most pronounced with some direct sun exposure; deep shade dulls the color pattern toward plain green. It is noticeably slower-growing and more compact than unvariegated asiatic jasmine, making it better suited to smaller-scale groundcover plantings, edging, rock gardens, and container use than as a fast-filling large-area groundcover. Once established it is drought-tolerant and needs little care beyond an occasional shearing to remove any reverted, solid-green shoots, which should be cut out promptly since they grow more vigorously than the variegated form and can overtake it.

common_name: Hidcote Blue Comfrey (Blue-Flowered Dwarf Comfrey Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich to average soil in partial to full shade in spring; Hidcote Blue is a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit selection of dwarf comfrey grown specifically for its flower color.

directions: Hidcote Blue is the most widely grown named selection of dwarf comfrey, chosen for its richer flower color: pendulous clusters of small, tubular flowers open from reddish-pink buds and mature to a clear blue-violet, a more saturated and ornamental color than the pale creamy-yellow to dull pale-blue flowers of the straight species. Flowers appear on arching stems in early spring, ahead of nearly every other shade perennial, over broad, hairy, dark-green, weed-suppressing foliage that persists as an effective groundcover mat through the rest of the season. Like the species, it spreads by rhizomes and modest self-sowing at a manageable pace and is much less aggressive than common comfrey. Excellent as a companion to hostas, ferns, and epimediums in dry to moderately moist shade, and notably more drought-tolerant than most comfrey species once established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown seedlings or a partly husked seed nut on its side with one-third buried in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; Maypan seedlings show some variability since it is an F1 hybrid rather than a true-breeding line.

directions: Maypan is a hybrid coconut developed in Jamaica by crossing the compact, precocious Malayan Dwarf with the larger, more vigorous Panama Tall, bred specifically to combine dwarf-parent resistance to lethal yellowing disease with taller-parent vigor, nut size, and yield after lethal yellowing devastated Jamaica's tall coconut plantations in the 20th century. It reaches an intermediate mature height, taller and more vigorous than pure Malayan Dwarf plantings but well short of unimproved tall varieties, and begins bearing somewhat later than Malayan Dwarf alone, typically five to seven years from planting. Maypan was widely distributed throughout Florida, the Caribbean, and other lethal-yellowing-affected regions starting in the 1970s-80s as the standard replacement variety for susceptible tall coconuts, though growers should note that resistance to lethal yellowing is relative rather than absolute and newer disease strains have reduced its reliability in some areas over time. Extremely frost-sensitive and restricted to the warmest USDA zones in the continental US.

common_name: Mrs. J. Bradshaw Geum (Semi-Double Scarlet-Red Avens)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mrs. J. Bradshaw pairs classically with the golden-yellow 'Lady Stratheden' for a two-tone geum display.

directions: Mrs. J. Bradshaw is one of the oldest and most widely grown scarlet geum cultivars, bearing brilliant scarlet-red, semi-double flowers held on branching, wiry stems above a mound of hairy, strawberry-like basal foliage from late spring into summer. It holds the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit and is traditionally planted alongside the golden-yellow Lady Stratheden as a classic cottage-garden combination. Deadhead spent flowers regularly to prolong bloom and encourage a repeat flush later in summer. Protect from hot afternoon sun in warm climates and ensure consistent moisture, since plants struggle and may die back in sustained summer heat. Divide congested clumps in early fall every 2-3 years to maintain vigor.
